newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Michelin seeks to trim some bulges.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Michelin seeks to trim some bulges.

text.p: Tyremaker Michelin aims to spruce up its balance sheet and bring debt more in line with equity without compromising projects to reinforce its position as an industry leader, company officials said this week.

The French group has carried a heavy debt load since the acquisition seven years ago of Uniroyal Goodrich that vaulted the group to the top ranks of the industry alongside Japan's Bridgestone and Goodyear.
It has brought its debt down from a peak of 35 billion french francs ($6.35 billion) in 1993 to 23 billion francs at the end of June 1996, but that was still nearly double the company's equity.

During a rare press tour of a Michelin tyre-testing facility in the southern Spanish town of Almeria this week, Chief Financial Officer Eric Bourdais de Charbonniere said the ideal debt-to-equity ratio for the company would be between 1 and 1.3.
He said Michelin was not considering a capital increase to bring down debt as stockmarket operators had been speculating.
"Our strategy is to reduce debt using cashflow," Bourdais de Charbonniere said. He said Michelin would resort to a capital increase only to fund an ambitious investment or acquisition.

Company officials said Michelin, which is well positioned in Europe and North America and has an 18 percent global market share, was studying projects in emerging economies as well as working on innovative products and new ways to make tyres.
The press tour itself, unusual for the traditionally secretive company, signalled a shift that may or may not be related to a possible succession at the helm or a share listing in New York.

Reports this week that the company was studying a U.S. listing, coming after a string of positive brokerage reports, drove the stock to a year high of 322.90 francs on Thursday. A spokesman said on Friday that no decision had been taken.
Michelin's stock, which has risen 14 percent this month, was down 0.5 percent at 319.30 francs on Friday afternoon.

The family-run enterprise has undergone a series of changes in the past year, notably a reorganisation announced by the three top bosses, who include Francois Michelin and his son Edouard, named after the founder of the firm.
Michelin, which pioneered the car tyre and patented the radial tyre in 1946, has also developed a new production method with potentially far-reaching implications.

A spokesman said Michelin had started making and selling tyres using a patented process code-named C3M and believed its rivals were still at the drawing board on the technology, which would allow the group to respond faster to shifts in demand.

He was reluctant to describe the new process in any detail but said it cuts the time it takes to go from raw materials to a finished tyre, and costs less. "We're trying to preserve the lead in C3M technology," he said.
Customers cannot tell the new tyres apart from those made using traditional methods, but wholesalers can, he said.

Michelin is currently producing fewer than one percent of its car tyres using the C3M process and does not envisage a large-scale substitution for the time being, he said. "We have to weigh financial and social issues."

Other breakthroughs include Michelin's energy-saving "Green" tyre rolled out in 1990, and the production last year of the first coloured tyres which the company views more as a technical exploit than a fad.
The spokesman said Michelin spends five percent of sales -- they totalled 66 billion francs in 1995 -- on research.
From its headquarters in Clermont-Ferrand in central France, Michelin is also studying distant markets offering faster growth rates in car and truck sales.
It has established a factory in China and has received authorisation from the Indian government to invest there.

"We don't produce in Russia but we'll have to establish a presence there," Bourdais de Charbonniere said. "You can't say you're a major global producer and ignore Russia or China or India or Indonesia."
($1=5.512 French Franc)
